semantics.note: Revision 2 restores 'in many other ways', 'pretty much' and 'frequently'. It is phrased as an observation but is a broad evaluative characterisation that cannot be tested.

contract.note: The contract is right that 'constant', 'frequently', 'rarely' and 'taking responsibility' have no defined measure. Adding thresholds would decide the result, so not_applicable is fair.

reviews.rationale: This is a sweeping evaluative comparison of two executives. It names no sample, frequency threshold or test of responsibility. Individual deadline examples could be checked separately, but they cannot settle the whole claim. The packet has no evidence items. Not adjudicable as stated.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Both antecedents (overload and overtrust) are kept. 'Inevitable' is firm language, so this is scorable as a conditional forecast with no deadline. It could also be read as a causal warning.

contract.note: The plain occurrence reading is ordinary and fair: serious errors will happen when both conditions hold. Requiring a post-publication operation with both conditions shown and linked to the error is reasonable. Earlier incidents are correctly excluded.

evidence.note: Later reporting on the Minab strike describes compressed review and misplaced reliance on Maven. But the strike was on Feb 28, 2026, before the post, so it cannot resolve the forecast.

Bloomberg reporting: investigators cite over-reliance on AI in the pre-publication Minab strike, and the report is unreleased. Later incidents are mentioned without overload or overtrust being established.
Earlier Semafor account blames human intelligence failures and notes uncertainty about review. It concerns the same pre-publication incident.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated. The packet shows no operation after March 8, 2026 in which both overload and overtrust are established and linked to a serious targeting error. The Minab incident came before the post. The antecedent is unknown for any later operation, and no conclusive event meets the early-resolution rule. An error-free period cannot refute the forecast.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the three characteristics and the Anthropic profit element. It drops the 'endless negative externalities' framing, which is rhetoric. 'Extremely difficult' is evaluative but has ordinary meaning.

contract.note: The plain reading of broad tendencies is ordinary. The February 2026 window is the evaluator's choice but a reasonable one. 'Profits from' has an unspecified accounting basis, so that part cannot be scored.

evidence.note: Company disclosure of a paid agentic model and its token prices. This shows neither task costs nor realised profit.
Company disclosure: Anthropic admits computer use lags skilled humans and that prompt-injection risk exists, while reporting improvement. This does not establish general unreliability.
Company demonstration: about $20k of API cost for a compiler, called cheap relative to human labour. This qualifies rather than establishes 'expensive', and is not a representative measure.
February preprint: tested defenses fail to secure agents or severely impair their utility. This supports the security-difficulty part for the workflows tested.
February preprint reports 0% attack success on a bounded benchmark. This qualifies the security part but does not refute broad difficulty.

reviews.rationale: Only the security component gets independent support (e4), and e5 qualifies it. Cost evidence is a single example in which the author calls the cost cheap relative to human work. Reliability evidence is a company disclosure only. Profit is unestablished, with no accounting basis. Nothing in the packet contradicts any part. The whole claim is not settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition drops the rhetorical 'notoriously' and keeps 'practically anything' and 'whether public domain or not'. Faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'practically anything' as describing breadth of sources, not near-total ingestion, is ordinary and fair given the hedge 'practically'. The contract also keeps copyright status separate from infringement.

evidence.note: Company disclosure: OpenAI says it trains on publicly available internet material and defends this as fair use, without limiting training to public-domain works.
Independent membership-inference study: OpenAI models memorised many in-copyright books. This corroborates use of copyrighted material, though not the acquisition source.
OpenAI filing lists crawl exclusions (paywalls, infringing sites). This qualifies a literal 'everything' reading but does not rebut broad use of copyrighted public material.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's own disclosure describes broad training on public internet material defended as fair use, not limited to the public domain. Independent research shows copyrighted books in its models. The reported exclusions narrow the scope but do not meet the contradiction condition. Under the fair breadth reading, the claim is supported.
